scenes.headline: The arrow [turns around]
scenes.caption: reverse uno
scenes.premise: Your server is public. Anyone can install it. Whoever holds the API key pays for every call it makes.
scenes.narration: Sampling flips the direction. Normally the client asks the server to do things, and every arrow points one way. ^Here the server turns round mid-tool and asks the client: you call the model for me, and send me back what it says. |The tool takes a c t x argument, which is the server's line back to whoever connected. |The call that does the asking is c t x dot session dot create message, ^and the key detail is that the client is the one holding an API key, so the client is the one who pays. The course calls it reverse uno, and the restaurant version is nicer: we prepped your ingredients, but would you cook the last step at your house — you've got a kitchen, and your own gas bill. |The generated text comes back as the result, %so your server stays cheap to run no matter how popular it gets, because the expensive part never happens on your machine.

scenes.headline: Still real, still [on a clock]
scenes.caption: status, honestly
scenes.premise: Sampling still works and stays in the spec for at least a year. It is also deprecated, and the spec says new code should not adopt it.
scenes.narration: Now the part the course you may have read doesn't cover, because the spec moved. ^As of protocol version twenty twenty six, dash oh seven, dash twenty eight, sampling is deprecated. It has not been removed — it stays in the specification for at least twelve months, and every existing client and server that uses it keeps working. ^But the official guidance is blunt: new implementations should not adopt it, and existing ones should migrate to calling an L L M provider's API directly. ^The earliest it becomes eligible for removal is a revision released on or after July twenty twenty seven. So why did we just spend a chapter on it? Because sampling is the clearest window into how this protocol thinks — a server that needs intelligence but refuses to hold a key — and because the code you inherit this year will be full of it. Learn it, recognise it, and don't start something new on it.
